g-pos-01.reason: Slot sits between 'were' and the past participle 'calculated', so only an adverb fits; 'automatic' cannot modify a verb.
g-pos-01.why: Textbook adverb-slot word-form item with a clean business stem; distractors are the standard noun/verb/adjective set.

g-pos-02.reason: 'seem' is a linking verb and takes an adjective complement; 'acceptably' would need a full verb, 'acceptance'/'accept' break the structure.
g-pos-02.why: Linking-verb + adjective is a staple Part 5 point and the stem reads like a real one.

g-pos-03.reason: 'The ______ of the factory' requires a noun; 'expansion' is the only noun. 'expanded' would need a following noun.

g-pos-04.reason: The relative clause 'who visited' needs a person noun: 'inspector'. 'inspection' is a thing and cannot take 'who'.
g-pos-04.why: Person-noun vs abstract-noun contrast is common on the real test.

g-pos-05.reason: 'a very ______ shutdown' needs an adjective; 'costly' is an adjective despite the -ly ending. 'costing shutdown' is not idiomatic.
g-pos-05.why: Nice -ly-adjective trap; exactly the kind of item that catches candidates who pattern-match on suffixes.

g-pos-06.reason: 'made it ______ easier' needs an adverb of degree modifying the comparative 'easier': 'considerably'.
g-pos-06.why: Adverb-modifying-comparative is a recurring real-test pattern.
g-pos-06.editorNote: Shares the consider- word family with v-family-01 (where 'considerable' is the key). Two items on the same family in one bank looks like recycling; swap one to another family.

g-tense-01.reason: A past-time frame ('shortly before the building was sold') requires simple past passive 'were replaced'; present perfect (A) clashes with a finished past reference, and (B) active 'replaced' has no object.
g-tense-01.why: Two-clause stem with a tense-clue and a passive/active contrast is realistic; 'so they are still under warranty' is a slightly artificial add-on.
g-tense-01.fix: Consider trimming the trailing clause or replacing it with a more natural detail ('...and the invoices are on file'), so the stem reads less like a constructed cue.

g-tense-02.reason: 'at the moment' fixes the present progressive: 'are investigating'.
g-tense-02.why: The cue 'at the moment' is more explicit than real items, which usually use 'currently' or rely on context and add a longer stem.
g-tense-02.fix: Replace 'at the moment' with 'currently' and lengthen the stem slightly, e.g. 'Our technicians ______ currently the cause of the network problem, so...'.

g-tense-03.reason: Time clause with 'Once' + future main clause takes present simple: 'completes'. 'will complete' is the standard trap.
g-tense-03.why: Classic time-clause tense item; stem and names look authentic.

g-tense-04.reason: 'since the spring of 2021' requires present perfect: 'has expanded'.
g-tense-04.why: Straight 'since' + present perfect item, very common on the real test.

g-tense-05.reason: 'By the time ... was completed' (past) requires past perfect 'had spent'.
g-tense-05.why: 'By the time' + past perfect is a standard pattern; distractors are the usual tense set.

g-connect-01.reason: The gap is followed by a noun phrase, so a preposition is needed; meaning (cause) selects 'because of' over 'despite'.
g-connect-01.why: Preposition-vs-conjunction with a meaning check is a real Part 5 staple.

g-connect-02.reason: A full clause follows ('they are on the site'), so a conjunction is required: 'while'. 'during'/'throughout' take nouns; 'meanwhile' is an adverb.

g-connect-03.reason: Contrast between higher price and continuing to order: 'however'. 'in spite of' needs a noun; 'whereas' cannot follow a semicolon as a stand-alone adverb.
g-connect-03.why: Conjunctive-adverb item is authentic in substance, though real items usually split into two sentences rather than using a semicolon.
g-connect-03.fix: Split into two sentences: '...its competitors. ______, we have decided...'.

g-connect-04.reason: Only 'unless' gives the intended exception meaning; 'if customers pay extra ... will not be shipped' reverses the logic; 'whether' does not fit.
g-connect-04.why: Good 'unless' item where the distractor 'if' is grammatical but illogical, just like real ones.

g-connect-05.reason: A clause follows, and 'still rose' signals concession: 'Even though'. 'Despite' needs a noun; 'Nevertheless' cannot introduce a subordinate clause.
g-connect-05.why: Standard concession item with the despite/even though contrast.

g-prep-01.reason: A deadline for a single action ('submitted') takes 'by'; 'until' is for continuing states.
g-prep-01.why: The by/until contrast is one of the most frequently tested prepositions.

g-prep-02.reason: Duration expressed as a number of days takes 'for'; 'during' takes a named period, not a quantity.

g-prep-03.reason: 'Upon completion of' is the fixed formal phrase meaning 'as soon as ... is completed'; 'Until/Since/Within completion' do not work.
g-prep-03.why: 'Upon completion' shows up in real TOEIC correspondence-style stems.

g-prep-04.reason: Present perfect 'has doubled' plus a past starting point requires 'Since'. 'During the merger ... has doubled' is not a natural pairing.
g-prep-04.why: Since + present perfect with a company-news stem is very TOEIC-like.

g-participle-01.reason: A pre-noun modifier meaning 'that has been updated' is the past participle 'updated'.
g-participle-01.editorNote: 'Web site' with a capital W is dated (older ETS house style); current usage is 'website'.

g-participle-02.reason: Reduced relative clause with active meaning ('companies that are participating') takes the present participle.
g-participle-02.why: Reduced-relative participle choice is a common medium-level item.

g-participle-03.reason: The center was built (passive), so the past participle 'Built' opens the reduced clause; 'Building in only six months' would mean the center is building something.
g-participle-03.why: Sentence-initial participle phrase is a standard real-test pattern.

g-participle-04.reason: Figures cause disappointment, so the -ing adjective 'disappointing' is required; 'disappointed' describes people.
g-participle-04.why: -ed/-ing adjective contrast is a stock item.

g-voice-01.reason: Badges are the recipients of the action and 'by the end of next week' points to the future: 'will be distributed'.
g-voice-01.why: Future passive with a deadline is a very common item.

g-voice-02.reason: 'rise' is intransitive; with no object and 'since', present perfect 'have risen' is the only fit. 'have raised' needs an object; 'have been risen' is not a real form.
g-voice-02.why: The rise/raise contrast is tested on the real exam; 'have been risen' is a non-existent form, and real distractors are usually genuine forms.
g-voice-02.fix: Replace 'have been risen' with a real but wrong form such as 'are rising' or 'had risen'.

g-voice-03.reason: 'by the board of directors' marks a passive agent, and the subject receives the sabbatical: 'was granted'.
g-voice-03.why: Passive with 'by' agent and a ditransitive verb is a solid medium item.

g-agree-01.reason: The head noun is plural 'projectors', not the nearer 'room' or 'floor': 'have'.
g-agree-01.why: Subject-verb agreement across an intervening prepositional phrase is a staple.

g-agree-02.reason: A gerund phrase subject ('Approving refund requests') is singular, and 'usually' signals present simple: 'takes'.
g-agree-02.why: Gerund-subject agreement with a plural noun nearby is a good realistic trap.

g-agree-03.reason: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, the plural 'two service contracts': 'require'.
g-agree-03.why: Proximity agreement is a legitimate rule but appears less often on the real test than simple head-noun agreement.
g-agree-03.fix: Optional: recast as an ordinary head-noun agreement item unless a proximity-rule item is deliberately wanted.

g-relative-01.reason: The relative word must show possession ('customers' subscriptions'): 'whose'.

g-relative-02.reason: 'two of ______' refers back to 'bids' (things) and is the object of 'of', so 'which'. 'whom' is for people.
g-relative-02.why: Quantifier + of + relative pronoun is a classic medium item.

g-relative-03.reason: 'acquired' needs an object; the relative pronoun supplies it: 'which'. 'where' would leave 'acquired' without an object.
g-relative-03.why: Non-restrictive relative clause after a place noun tempting 'where' is very authentic.

g-pronoun-01.reason: The company is singular and a possessive determiner is needed before 'return policy': 'its'.
g-pronoun-01.why: Its/it/itself is a common easy item.

g-pronoun-02.reason: 'those of' stands for 'the delivery times of'; plural antecedent 'delivery times' selects 'those' over 'that'.
g-pronoun-02.why: The that/those-of comparison item is frequently tested.

g-pronoun-03.reason: The gap is the subject of 'took' and replaces 'my reimbursement request': the possessive pronoun 'mine'.
g-pronoun-03.why: Possessive-pronoun item with a clear parallel structure.

g-toing-01.why: Verb + to-infinitive is a stock pattern.
g-toing-01.editorNote: 'Leeds' is a real UK city; the bank otherwise uses invented place names. Harmless, but real items usually avoid recognisable places.

g-toing-02.reason: 'In addition to' is a preposition, so a gerund follows: 'editing'.
g-toing-02.why: The 'in addition to + -ing' trap is well represented on the real test.

g-toing-03.reason: 'let + object' takes the bare infinitive: 'carry out'.
g-toing-03.why: Causative 'let' + bare infinitive is a real medium point.

g-compare-01.reason: 'much ______ than' requires a comparative adjective after 'is': 'cheaper'.

g-compare-02.reason: Parallel comparative construction 'The earlier ..., the more ...' requires 'the more'.

g-compare-03.why: 'superior to' is a classic collocation trap on the real test.

g-quantity-01.reason: 'information' is uncountable and the sentence is negative: 'much'. 'many/several/a few' need count nouns.
g-quantity-01.why: Count/uncount quantifier item with a very common TOEIC noun.

g-quantity-02.reason: Only 'Most' can stand before 'of the applicants' with a plural verb; 'Almost' is an adverb, 'Every' cannot take 'of', 'Much' is for uncount.

g-quantity-03.reason: 'equipment' is uncountable (confirmed by 'most of it'), so only 'a great deal of' fits; the other three need plural count nouns.
g-quantity-03.why: Good item: all four quantifiers look plausible until the learner registers 'equipment' as uncountable.

g-parallel-02.why: Correlative pair item; the 'nor' cue makes it easy, as on the real test.

g-parallel-03.reason: 'must register ... and ______' coordinates two bare infinitives after 'must': 'keep'.
g-parallel-03.why: Parallelism after a modal is a common medium item.

g-mandative-01.reason: 'requested that' triggers the mandative subjunctive (base form) regardless of the singular subject: 'submit'.
g-mandative-01.why: Subjunctive after 'request' is one of the most reliably tested Part 5 points.

g-mandative-02.reason: 'It is essential that' takes the subjunctive; the negative subjunctive is 'not be'. 'will not be' is not standard after 'essential that'.
g-mandative-02.why: Negative subjunctive is a step harder than the usual positive base-form item but is still within the real test's range.
g-mandative-02.fix: If the set already has g-mandative-01, consider making this one an adjective-triggered positive subjunctive instead to avoid two subjunctive items; otherwise keep as the hard item.

g-conditional-01.reason: Third-conditional inversion: 'Had the supplier notified us ..., we would have found'. 'Should/Were' do not combine with a past participle; 'Unless' + past simple + 'would have' is ungrammatical.
g-conditional-01.why: Inverted conditional is a genuine upper-band Part 5 item.

g-conditional-02.reason: 'Not until' at the front forces subject-auxiliary inversion; with the bare infinitive 'begin' the auxiliary must be 'did'.
g-conditional-02.why: Negative-adverbial inversion appears on the real test but rarely; combined with a past-time clause this is at the top of the difficulty range.
g-conditional-02.fix: Keep as the single hardest item, but do not add more inversion items; alternatively replace 'Not until' with a more common 'Only after ... did' structure.

v-collocation-01.reason: 'meet a deadline' is the fixed collocation; 'match/catch/suit a deadline' are not idiomatic.

v-collocation-02.reason: 'take effect' is the idiom; 'come/go' need 'into', 'make' does not collocate.
v-collocation-02.why: 'take effect' is a standard policy-memo item.

v-collocation-04.reason: 'keep a close eye on' is the idiom; 'hold/take/set an eye' are not.

v-collocation-05.reason: 'strike a balance' is the idiom; 'pull/run/lift a balance' are not.
v-collocation-05.why: Slightly less frequent idiom, good medium item.

v-collocation-06.reason: 'an overwhelming majority' is the fixed collocation; 'overriding' pairs with 'concern/priority', not 'majority'.
v-collocation-06.why: Prefix-sharing distractors are exactly how real vocab items are built.

v-synonym-01.reason: A percentage earned per contract on top of base salary is a 'commission'.

v-synonym-02.reason: 'lends ... to staff ... free of charge' rules out 'rents'; 'borrows' has the wrong direction; 'donates' is not temporary.
v-synonym-02.why: The phrase 'free of charge and for up to two weeks' spells out the answer more than a real item would.
v-synonym-02.fix: Drop 'free of charge' and let 'for up to two weeks at a time' plus 'lends' carry the meaning; keep 'rents' as the tempting distractor.

v-synonym-03.reason: 'incur charges' is the collocation; 'suffer/undergo/endure' do not take 'charges'.
v-synonym-03.why: 'incur' is a real TOEIC-level word and the hotel context is authentic.

v-synonym-04.reason: The whole 'comprises' the parts; 'consists' needs 'of'; 'composes/constitutes' run the other way (parts compose the whole).
v-synonym-04.why: Legitimate usage item, but the four near-synonyms make it harder than most real vocab items.
v-synonym-04.fix: Consider replacing 'composes' with a clearly different verb (e.g. 'contains'), keeping 'consists' as the main trap.

v-synonym-05.reason: A 40 percent jump that then holds is a 'markedly' increased level; 'steadily' contradicts a single jump, 'temporarily' contradicts 'for the rest of the year', 'slightly' contradicts 40 percent.
v-synonym-05.why: Adverb item where the participial clause disambiguates, as in real items.

v-synonym-06.reason: 'extend a lease' is the collocation; 'expand/enlarge/stretch' do not apply to contract duration.

v-business-01.reason: Flight times and hotel addresses are in an 'itinerary'.

v-business-02.reason: A document 'payable within 30 days' is an 'invoice'; an estimate is not payable, a receipt follows payment.

v-business-03.reason: 'postponed until next Thursday' is the only option that takes 'until' a later date.

v-business-04.reason: Costs are 'deducted from' salary; 'reduced from' does not mean subtraction of an item.
v-business-04.why: Alliterative distractors mirror the real test's style.

v-business-05.reason: 'reimbursed for fuel' is the payroll term.
v-business-05.why: High-frequency TOEIC word with r- distractors, very authentic.

v-business-06.reason: 'absorb the extra cost' means to bear it; 'adopt/attach/acquire' do not collocate.

v-family-01.reason: 'a considerable amount' is the collocation; 'considerate' means thoughtful.
v-family-01.editorNote: Same word family as g-pos-06; see that item.

v-family-02.reason: 'sensitive information' is the fixed phrase; 'sensible' means reasonable.

v-family-03.reason: 'their respective regions' = each person's own region.
v-family-03.why: 'respective' is a regular TOEIC vocabulary target.

v-family-04.reason: 'industrious' = hardworking; the others relate to industry.
v-family-04.why: Word-family item at the right level.

v-family-05.reason: 'comprehensible to' = understandable; 'comprehensive' means thorough and does not take 'to' in this sense.

v-family-06.reason: 'every imaginable size' is the idiom; 'imaginary' = not real.

l-qr-01.reason: 'Where' question; (B) gives a location. (A) answers 'who', (C) answers 'when'.

l-qr-02.reason: Statement of a problem; (C) explains it indirectly (someone else has the file open). (A) repeats 'sales/quarter', (B) plays on 'drive'.
l-qr-02.why: Indirect reply to a statement is exactly the harder Part 2 type the real test uses.

l-qr-03.reason: Alternative question; (A) implies 'train' by mentioning expensive parking. (B) answers 'when', (C) is a 'train/trained' sound trap.
l-qr-03.why: Indirect answer to an or-question is authentic.
l-qr-03.fix: Use 'center' (US spelling) for consistency with the rest of the bank unless the transcript is deliberately marked as a British speaker.
l-qr-03.editorNote: 'centre' is British spelling; irrelevant when spoken but inconsistent in the script.

l-qr-04.reason: Negative yes/no question; (C) answers 'no, expected Friday'. (A) is a 'come in' sound trap, (B) repeats 'name'.
l-qr-04.why: Negative-question item with sound and word repeats, very realistic.

l-qr-05.reason: Tag question; (A) confirms and adds detail. (B) plays on 'present', (C) is past tense about a future meeting.
l-qr-05.why: Tag-question item; the 'present' pun is a standard distractor type.

l-qr-06.reason: 'When' question; (A) indirectly says 'not yet'. (B) answers 'yes' to a wh-question, (C) repeats 'list'.

l-qr-07.reason: Offer; (B) indirectly declines (not ready yet). (A) answers 'where', (C) repeats 'client'.
l-qr-07.why: Indirect refusal of an offer is well represented on the real test.

l-qr-08.reason: Directions request; (C) explains the speaker cannot help. (A) 'Yes' to a how-question, (B) confuses 'how do I get to' with commuting.
l-qr-08.why: 'I don't know' style indirect reply is a recurring real pattern.

overall.grammar: All 52 grammar items resolve to a single defensible key; I could not make a second option work on any of them, including the British/American and informal-usage angles (mandative 'will submit', 'during' + present perfect, neither/nor proximity). Coverage of the classic Part 5 points is good: word form, tense, passive, agreement, relative and possessive pronouns, gerund/infinitive, comparatives, quantifiers, correlatives, subjunctive, inverted conditionals. Stems are business-register and mostly the right length, though a few are shorter and more cue-driven than real ones (g-tense-02). Minor editorial issues: 'Web site' (dated), a non-existent verb form used as a distractor (g-voice-02), a semicolon construction (g-connect-03), a real UK city name (g-toing-01), and the consider- family used twice across g-pos-06/v-family-01.
overall.vocab: All 24 vocabulary items have one clear key. The collocation and word-family items are the strongest and read like real ETS items (v-business-05, v-collocation-06, v-family-06). v-synonym-02 over-signals the answer with 'free of charge'; v-synonym-04 (comprise/compose/constitute) is a harder usage item than most real vocab questions but is not ambiguous. What is missing is the real test's harder type where all four options are the same part of speech and all semantically plausible until the learner reads the whole sentence; here most distractors can be eliminated on collocation alone.
overall.listening: All 26 listening keys are unambiguous. Part 2 has a good mix of wh-, yes/no, negative, tag, alternative and statement prompts with indirect answers and sound/word-repeat distractors, which is exactly the current test's profile. Part 3/4 questions use the current formats (intention questions with a quoted line, why-mention, next action) and the paraphrases are natural. Gaps versus the real test: no three-speaker conversation, no graphic-based question in Part 3 or Part 4, and the scripts mix British and American lexis ('lifts', 'centre') while the printed options are American.
overall.mix: The spread skews easier than a real form. Grammar comes out roughly 28 easy / 21 medium / 3 hard out of 52; vocab 14 / 9 / 1 of 24; listening 9 easy / 17 medium / 0 hard of 26. A real Part 5 set has a heavier medium core and a handful of genuinely hard items with long two-clause stems; a real vocab set has more items where every option is grammatically fine. Real listening has a few harder Part 3/4 sets (three speakers, graphics, faster overlap of details). Nothing tests verb + preposition combinations (comply with, rely on), 'as ... as', adverb placement, or formal correspondence phrases ('in accordance with', 'on behalf of'), all common on the real Part 5. Also missing are a Part 1 photo description and Part 6/7 material, if the bank is meant to sample the whole test.
